subject: Fitting global detection function to a subset of survey strata

messages.author: 77fa2bc3ece64945
messages.subject: Fitting global detection function to a subset of survey strata
parts:
Hi there,

I've been using the Distance package in R to analyse line transect data from six survey strata.  Three of these strata represent a protected area.  I want to use the 'global' detection function (I pooled data) to get estimates and a CV for just the protected area.  I get that this can be summed for some values (mean abdundance, for example) but I don't understand how to do this for the CV, LCL and UCL.  I hoped someone could provide me with a pointer?

I've also been struggling to find how to predict values back to the transects using R.  Is there a tutorial that I have missed?

Thanks in advance and happy to provide more details,

Gwili

messages.author: 09607d3641d0afd1
messages.subject: Fwd: Fitting global detection function to a subset of survey strata
parts:
Gwili

Performing calculations from stratum-specific estimates of density or abundance takes a bit of thinking, particularly regarding measures of precision.

If your interest lies in the abundance in the protected area, the simplest solution would be to simply analyse the data only from those three strata. Is there a reason why you cannot do that?

If you reject that approach, you need to do more difficult analyses of the stratum-specific estimates for the 3 strata of interest. First, the density estimate for the protected area is a weighted average, weighting by the size of each stratum. Examine slide 5 of this lecture on stratification from our online workshop materials:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-2%20Stratification.pdf

Calculating precision of the weighted average of the stratum-specific abundances is more complex. Here is the formula for variance of the sum of geographically-defined strata (sorry for the poor quality):

from that formula for variance, you can go on to derive a CV, and subsequently confidence intervals.

I'm a bit uncomfortably with the use of a pooled detection function to then produce stratum-specific density/abundance estimates. This procedure produces bias in the stratum-specific estimates as shown in this paper

Rexstad, E., Buckland, S., Marshall, L., & Borchers, D. (2023). Pooling robustness in distance sampling: Avoiding bias when there is unmodelled heterogeneity. Ecology and Evolution, 13, e9684. https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9684 

This can be resolved by either a) not using strata for you estimate of protected area abundance or b) including a covariate for stratum (as shown in the above reference).

Finally regarding transect-specific estimates. These estimates are produced in the object created by the ds() function. Recognise the transect-specific estimates do not have uncertainty associated with encounter rate variability in your study. If the object created by the call to the ds() function was called myestimates, the transect-specific abundance estimates are found in myestimates$dht$individuals$Nhat.by.sample

Let me know if you have questions about this.

messages.author: 77fa2bc3ece64945
messages.subject: Re: Fitting global detection function to a subset of survey strata
parts:
Hi Eric and thanks for your swift reply,

Having the protected area specific abundance estimate is important to compare to prior surveys, that did not survey the three additional strata in this most recent survey.

I ran detection function selection for the just the protect area strata.  The best fitting model had a different adjustment and produces an abundance estimate that was 23% higher than the summed abundance for the protected area from the six strata model.  This estimate is also higher than the abundance estimate across all six strata, which is not ideal for messaging.  Using the same detection function as for the whole strata, which does not fit as well, produces an abundance estimate 11% higher, which is still higher than the summed abundance for the protected area from the six strata model. 

When I try not using strata, this produces abundance estimates 40% higher for the best fitting model and 24% when using the same model that produced the best fit for the full data set.

Thanks for your paper, I will try fitting the strata as a covariate shortly and feedback.

Cheers also for the pointer on finding the transect specific estimates

Best,

Gwili
